title: The Silence of the Bells
shortDescription: Thirty years after a flood silenced the bells of San Jerónimo del Viento and took his brother’s life, Gabriel returns to sell his father’s house. A promise carved into the bell tower forces him to revisit his memories and discover that faith does not erase loss, but it can open a path toward truth, responsibility, and reconciliation.
description: Thirty years after a flood silenced the bells of San Jerónimo del Viento and took his brother’s life, Gabriel returns to sell his father’s house. chapters.title: The Town That Forgot How to Listen
chapters.content:
The bus dropped Gabriel Salvatierra off in front of the old station in San Jerónimo del Viento, where the tin roof still rattled even when there was no breeze. Fifteen years had passed since his last visit. The square still had its crooked plane trees, its dry fountain, and the bakery on the corner; only the bell tower seemed smaller. Perhaps that was because, as a child, he had seen it as a mountain, or because silence had gradually robbed it of its height.

The bells had not rung in thirty years. The younger residents knew them only from photographs: two bronze bells, one large and one small, hanging in a gray stone tower. Once, they had marked festivals, funerals, working hours, and the start of the harvest. After the flood, no one ever pulled the ropes again. There was no written prohibition. There was something more effective: every family had its own reason for not wanting to hear them.

Gabriel had returned because his father, Tomás, had died. The funeral had taken place while a storm kept the only road from the capital closed. His aunt Rebeca, who met him outside the house, did not reproach him for his absence.

“You arrived in time to decide what to do with his things,” she said, placing the key in his palm. “We don't always arrive in time for everything else.”

The house smelled of limewash, machine oil, and ground coffee. Tomás had been a blacksmith, a locksmith, and, in earlier days, the man responsible for maintaining the bell tower. A worn file, two iron clamps, and a small drawing of the bells' mechanisms lay on the workbench. The workshop chair faced the window, as though his father had spent his final years watching over a tower he could not repair.

Gabriel had come to sell. He was a metal-structures technician and had learned to assess damage without listening to the stories of those who suffered it. In his head, he calculated the house's selling price, the land's value, and the hours it would take to empty the workshop. He had a life in the city, a twelve-year-old daughter named Julia, and a recent separation he almost never spoke about. San Jerónimo was the place where he had lost his brother and where he had decided to stop believing in anything that promised protection.

Mateo, three years older than Gabriel, had died when the Río Blanco burst its banks. Gabriel remembered dirty water battering the walls and his father running toward the tower instead of coming home. He also remembered the sound of the bells mingling with the shouts from the bridge. For three decades, he had distilled those images into a single accusation: Tomás had chosen to save the bell tower rather than search for Mateo.

At dusk, a woman knocked on the door. She carried a folder of photographs and wore a yellow hard hat much too large for her head. She introduced herself as Irene Robles, a science teacher and coordinator of a small neighborhood committee.

“Your father used to help us inspect the cracks in the tower,” she said. “We know you work with metal. We wanted to ask whether you could look at the supports before the municipality decides to close off access.”

Gabriel shook his head.

“I didn't come back to repair a church.”

“I'm not here on behalf of a church, either,” Irene replied, without raising her voice. “The staircase leads to the water reservoir, and children pass through there. If the structure gives way, someone could get hurt.”

That made him listen. Irene spoke of no symbols, promises, or miracles. She showed him a photograph: a crack ran across the base of the arch supporting the larger bell. Another showed a piece of corroded iron that had fallen onto the tower floor. Gabriel promised to inspect the place the next day, once and only once, for safety's sake. Irene thanked him without treating it as a victory.

Before leaving, she pointed to the drawing on the workbench.

“Tomás used to say a bell isn't the voice of a town. It's only a tool. The voice comes from the people, when they know what they want to say.”

Gabriel waited until she had shut the door before crumpling the paper slightly. It irritated him to hear strangers repeating his father's words. He was also unsettled by the familiar handwriting of the measurements: a firm line at first, shakier in the margins, as though Tomás had kept drawing even after his hands had begun to fail him.

He went out to buy bread. Near the old bridge, now replaced by a concrete footbridge, he found a plaque bearing nine names. Mateo Salvatierra was the fourth. A little girl was laying yellow flowers at the foot of the memorial while her grandfather waited a few paces away. Gabriel did not approach. He stood looking at the river, now narrow and calm, unable to reconcile it with that night.

When he returned home, his phone displayed a message from Julia: “Are you okay, Dad?” He wanted to reply with his usual “Everything's fine,” but the words felt heavy. He wrote, “Today I saw a place I was afraid to remember. We'll talk tomorrow.” His daughter replied with a heart and a question: “Will you tell me what Uncle Mateo was like?”

Gabriel turned off the screen. He had never told her anything about his brother beyond a date and a photograph. He went to bed without unpacking his suitcase. Outside, the wind slipped through the silent arches of the bell tower. No bells rang, but for the first time the silence did not seem empty: it seemed full of words someone had left unfinished.

chapters.title: The Promise Carved into the Bell Tower
chapters.content:
The following morning, Gabriel climbed the tower with Irene and old Eusebio, the mason who had tended the town's walls for forty years. The staircase was narrow and covered in dust. Every wooden step answered with a different creak. A severed rope hung on the first landing; on the second, a glassless window let in the scent of fig trees.

“Don't touch that beam,” Gabriel warned as Eusebio rested a hand on a support. “Moisture has eaten away at its cross-section. And that bolt wouldn't withstand a strong vibration.”

The old man obeyed immediately. Irene took photographs, recorded measurements, and waited while Gabriel finished examining the anchorages. The larger bell had a small notch near its rim. The smaller one was intact, although its clapper lay on a wooden board. Neither could be rung without substantial work.

“Can they be repaired?” Irene asked.

“The question is whether they ought to ring. Securing the tower is one thing; subjecting it to dynamic loads it can no longer withstand is another.”

Irene wrote down both remarks. Gabriel was grateful she made no attempt to persuade him.

While lifting a sheet of metal, he discovered a section of wood beneath the dust, protected by a small covering. When he removed it, he found numbers, dates, and marks scratched into the surface with a pointed tool. They were Tomás's. Gabriel recognized the way his father formed the letter l, leaving it open at the bottom. Alongside the technical notes was a sentence enclosed in a rectangle: “If they ever ring again, no one should have to guess which way to run.”

Gabriel read it aloud without meaning to. Eusebio bowed his head.

“He wrote that after the flood,” he explained. “He insisted that if the town ever used the bells again, the signals for a celebration and a danger had to be different.”

“My father was the one who rang them that night,” Gabriel said. “People went out into the streets because of him.”

Eusebio did not argue.

“Yes. He pulled the rope. What that act meant has divided us for thirty years.”

Behind the covering lay a sheet of waxed paper bearing an old diagram. Gabriel unfolded it carefully: one long peal meant a gathering in the square; three quick strikes meant the river was rising; five meant fire. But someone had crossed out the instructions in the margin with charcoal: “Useless if everyone remembers a different signal.” Beneath that, in Tomás's handwriting, was a new proposal: hand-operated alarms on the higher streets, signs along the roads, and evacuation drills before any bell was restored.

Gabriel felt something shift in his memories. In his recollection, Tomás had never admitted making mistakes. Yet here was a plan written by someone who had considered them, even if that did not absolve him of responsibility.

“Why didn't he do anything?” Gabriel asked.

Eusebio looked toward the open bell tower.

“He proposed changes. The town council said the bridge and the houses had to be repaired first. Then the mayors changed. Then another drought came. People were exhausted. So was he.”

On the way down, Irene showed him a municipal file. One page contained a petition signed by Tomás and thirty-four residents calling for an evacuation route along the eastern hillside. It had never been allocated a budget. Another page recorded a recent inspection: the tower was to remain closed to the public until temporary reinforcements were installed.

“We're not going to ring the bells out of nostalgia,” Irene made clear. “We want a safe place and a plan that works. If we end up without bells, we'll have to accept that, too.”

Gabriel examined the stamps and dates. From a professional standpoint, the requirements were obvious: close off access, stabilize the wall, inspect the anchorage, run the calculations. On a personal level, it was still unbearable.

That afternoon, looking for a tape measure in the workshop, he found a metal box of screws sorted by size. A label on the lid read: “For when Gabriel wants to understand why a part fails.” Inside were no apologies or confessions, only nuts, washers, and a small notebook of load tests. It was precisely the awkward sort of gift Tomás would have given him while he was alive.

Rebeca arrived with a plate of stew. She noticed the drawings on the table.

“You've been up in the tower.”

“I only checked that it wasn't about to collapse.”

“That's what your father said at first. Then he'd spend nights trying to find a way to straighten it.”

Gabriel closed the notebook.

“Why did he never talk to me about Mateo?”

“Because whenever he tried, you walked away. And later, because he got used to not trying. Neither of those things was right.”

There was no reproach in Rebeca's voice. That was precisely why it hurt more.

That night, Gabriel called Julia. He told her Mateo had always been the first to reach the river each summer, that he made little boats from pine bark, and that once he had taught a cat to follow him all the way to the bakery. Julia laughed. Then she asked:

“Was he brave?”

Gabriel looked at the old diagram of the warning signals.

“Yes,” he answered. “But I think I spent far too long not wanting to know what he actually did.”

After hanging up, he read the sentence carved into the tower again. His father had not promised to bring back the past. He had promised that if that metal ever found its voice again, it would never confuse anyone. For the first time, Gabriel wondered whether repairing the bell tower had less to do with making bronze ring than with taking responsibility for the silence that had followed.

chapters.title: The Wounds No One Wanted to Heal
chapters.content:
The first community meeting took place at the school. Irene hung two maps on a wall: one showing the town as it was now, the other drawn shortly before the flood. Gabriel brought photographs of the damaged supports. They discussed cracks, budgets, and permits until a woman in the back row raised her hand.

“That's all very well, but I don't want to hear those bells again,” she said. “My sister ran toward the bridge when they started ringing. She never came back.”

Her name was Adela Montoro. Her hands were clasped around her handbag, and her voice seemed to be made of the same stone as the tower. No one contradicted her. Across the room, a man declared that the bells had saved his parents because they had woken them in time. Both statements were true. Gabriel was surprised that no one had ever found a way to say them together.

“We haven't come here to vote on people's memories,” Irene interjected. “We've come to listen to what was missing then and what must be in place now so that no one is confused again.”

Adela stood and walked out. Gabriel followed her, not to persuade her, but because he recognized in her stride the urge to escape before someone mistook pain for stubbornness.

“My brother died, too,” he said, keeping a respectful distance.

Adela looked at him wearily.

“I know. You're Tomás's son. You don't need to explain what you lost. But don't ask me to forgive a sound just because other people want to celebrate.”

“I won't.”

She nodded. Then, in an unexpected gesture, she took a faded photograph from her handbag. It showed children beside the river, their knees muddy and their arms raised. Gabriel recognized Mateo at one side, holding a ball under his arm.

“My sister took it two weeks before she died,” Adela said. “You can keep it if you promise not to turn them into saints. They were kids. They laughed, fought, and got scared. They deserved to grow old.”

Gabriel accepted the photograph. The word “saints” stayed with him for hours. He had turned Mateo into a motionless statue of goodness, and his father into its opposite. Neither had been able to defend himself against such narrow ways of being remembered.

At noon, he went to Eusebio's house. The mason spread a map across the kitchen table and pointed to the old wooden bridge.

“The water rose in less than an hour. The river carried logs downstream and blocked the mill crossing. Tomás rang the fire alarm because it was the only signal everyone recognized. He thought it would get them out of their houses.”

“Then why did he use it if there was a code for flooding?”

“Because the new code was never properly taught. The older people learned one signal; the younger ones, another. I was up on the high road, shouting for people not to go down to the bridge, but my voice couldn't reach the square.”

Eusebio hesitated before continuing. He said Mateo, then sixteen, had helped guide several families toward the hillside. When he learned that two children were still on the other side, he went back with some of the other neighbors. The current slammed against the bridge piers. No one ordered him to cross. No one could stop him.

“Your father came down from the tower as soon as he saw people heading toward the river,” Eusebio said. “He reached the bridge. I saw him wade in up to his chest. We had to pull him out by force because the current was carrying him away.”

Gabriel gripped the edge of the table.

“He never told me that.”

“Neither did I. I thought it was his place to tell you. We divided the silence among ourselves as though it were a form of respect.”

Gabriel left without thanking him. This information did not erase Tomás's poor decision to sound an ambiguous signal, nor the tragedy caused by the badly maintained bridge. Nor did it turn Mateo's death into something that had to happen. It merely made the simple version Gabriel had lived with impossible to sustain.

He visited Adela in the square. He showed her the map and told her what Eusebio remembered, without demanding a response.

“My father could make mistakes, too,” he acknowledged. “He thought he was warning everyone. He never checked whether they understood.”

Adela listened in silence.

“My sister knew how to swim,” she said at last. “For years I told myself that meant she should have survived. As if knowing how to swim could save you from a river full of trees. Sometimes we need someone to blame because the other explanation is too much to bear.”

“Have you forgiven him?”

“Some mornings, yes. Other mornings, no. Please don't make me choose a final answer.”

At dusk, Gabriel entered the small chapel adjoining the square. He had not attended a religious service since his mother's funeral. He sat in the back pew, more from exhaustion than devotion. An elderly woman was struggling to turn on the lights. On the wall was an old inscription: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.”

Gabriel was not sure he believed in comfort. He studied the worn wood and thought of Mateo: not the hero of the stories, but the boy who had taught him to hop from stone to stone in the river and who kept sweets in his pockets even though their mother scolded him for it.

“I don't know how to talk to you,” he murmured, unsure whether he was addressing God, his brother, or his own memory. “And I don't want anyone telling me it all happened for a reason.”

No one answered. He stayed there a while. When he got up, the elderly woman tending the lights offered him a glass of water. She did not ask what was wrong or offer any words of consolation. Gabriel drank it and stepped out into the square, where children were still playing despite the cold. He realized that, for that evening, it was enough that the world did not demand an explanation from him.

chapters.title: When Believing Feels Impossible
chapters.content:
Gabriel's report was unequivocal: the tower needed stabilization at its north corner, new metal connections, and a foundation inspection. Ringing either bell before those repairs would have been irresponsible. Irene presented the report to the town council along with a proposal for signs, evacuation routes, and community training.

The reply came on a page containing three paragraphs. The annual budget made no provision for restoration work. The building would be fenced off. Residents could raise private funds, provided they hired licensed professionals and obtained the necessary permits. There was no money for the project, and no political enthusiasm for discussing it.

Eusebio read the reply and laid his glasses on the table.

“It's not the end,” he said, “but it looks a lot like it.”

Gabriel was due to leave the next day. He had found a buyer for the workshop and needed to return to his job. Besides, Julia was expecting him that weekend to take her to a museum he had promised to visit months earlier. He packed Tomás's tools into boxes, separating those that could still be used from those that were beyond repair. One wrench bore a streak of blue paint. He remembered using it as a child, holding a part steady while Mateo turned the crank. He slipped it into his pocket.

Irene appeared at dusk. She did not ask him to stay.

“The school can run an evacuation drill even if the bell tower remains closed,” she explained. “Everything else will have to wait.”

“That's the sensible thing to do.”

“Doing the sensible thing can hurt, Gabriel. That doesn't make it any less sensible.”

He offered her coffee, and for the first time they talked about something other than the tower. Irene explained that she had returned to town to care for her mother after an accident. She had expected to stay six months and had now been there eight years. She loved teaching children to measure rainfall, observe insects, and understand why maps were incomplete promises: they were useful only when someone learned how to use them.

“Do you still believe?” Gabriel asked, gesturing toward the chapel outside the window.

Irene took her time answering.

“I do, but not the way I used to. My mother never regained her mobility. I prayed many times that she would. Now I usually pray that we'll have patience, resources, and people who won't disappear when we grow tired. I don't think that's a lesser kind of faith, even if some days it feels terribly small.”

Gabriel looked at his grease-stained hands.

“I prayed for my brother to come back. I was thirteen. After that, I decided I would never ask for anything again.”

“That's a wound, too,” Irene said. “I have no right to close it with a sentence.”

Those words seemed more honest to him than any of the speeches people had used to console him.

That night, a storm broke over the valley. It did not cause a flood, but the drains filled with leaves and a small irrigation ditch overflowed near the school. At eleven o'clock, Irene called Gabriel. A low wall had collapsed, and water was starting to enter the storeroom where they kept books and electrical equipment. There were volunteers, but they lacked tools and someone who could inspect a leaning utility pole before anyone moved it.

Gabriel could have refused. His boxes were packed, his vehicle keys lay on the table, and he had no formal responsibility. Instead, he grabbed his raincoat and went.

They worked for three hours in the rain. Irene organized the neighbors to carry the books to a dry place; Eusebio marked off the unsafe area; Gabriel temporarily secured the pole and insisted that no one approach it until the electric utility had inspected it. Others cleared the ditch from its upper end, following clear instructions. There were no acts of heroism, only tired hands carrying out specific tasks.

When the water receded, they found a student's drawing notebook lying open on a table. The child had drawn a map of the neighborhood with arrows pointing toward the hillside and a note in a child's handwriting: “If it rains a lot, don't go to the bridge.” Gabriel held it for a moment. That child had learned in a classroom what the adults had failed to pass on thirty years earlier.

He returned home in the early hours. A message from Julia was waiting: “Are you coming? It's okay if we change the museum trip, but tell me the truth.” He sat down before replying. Over the past few years, he had used work as a respectable excuse for missing so many things. He did not want his daughter to inherit that habit.

He called her, even though he knew the ringing phone might wake her mother. Julia answered sleepily. Gabriel explained what had happened and suggested picking her up on Sunday without canceling the outing.

“Why are you helping people there?” she asked.

“Because they needed someone who knew how to secure a piece of metal. And because other people did their part.”

“That sounds like what you tell me when we fix my bicycle.”

Gabriel smiled for the first time in many hours.

Before dawn, he sent Irene a simple plan for temporary reinforcement and a list of materials with approximate costs. He made clear that everything would need professional verification and permission before any work was carried out. Then he added a message: “I can't promise to rebuild the tower. But I can help with the safety project and teach the neighbors how to read the warning signs.”

The sale contract remained unsigned on the table. This was no solemn act of conversion. It was a small, weary decision: to postpone the quickest solution for a few weeks until he could work out what responsibility he was prepared to accept. Gabriel thought that perhaps faith did not begin with a dazzling certainty. Perhaps, for someone like him, it began when he stopped running away every time a question remained unanswered.

chapters.title: The Night Before the First Chime
chapters.content:
Six weeks passed. The tower remained fenced off while an independent engineer inspected the foundations and approved a partial stabilization plan. A small community fund, contributions from former residents, and a municipal allocation for disaster prevention made it possible to repair the damaged wall. The larger bell was secured against movement: it still needed work that no one could afford. The smaller bell, however, could be mounted on a new frame, isolated from the old structure, in the side courtyard. It would be tested there first, with no audience and with measuring instruments in place.

Gabriel had not designed the system alone. The engineer calculated the supports; Eusebio helped prepare the base; Irene coordinated information for the residents; and two young apprentices cleaned the metal under supervision. Everyone signed off on their own part of the work. They also agreed that no bell would replace modern alarms or radio announcements. The school taught children two safe evacuation routes, easy-to-read maps were posted, and drills were conducted for people with limited mobility.

Not everyone applauded. Adela attended the meetings but did not want to take part in the ceremony. Her presence, even in disagreement, forced the committee to ask questions it would have been easier to avoid: Who would warn visitors? What would people who could not hear do? How could they prevent a celebratory sound from being mistaken for an emergency signal?

The committee adopted a written rule: the smaller bell would be rung only for celebrations announced in advance, never as a warning of danger. Before each ringing, the community would be informed through loudspeakers, notices, and messages. Emergency procedures would be separate, easy to understand, and reinforced through repeated drills. Gabriel insisted that the rule be displayed beside the courtyard, not filed away in a drawer.

On the afternoon before the ceremony, Julia arrived in San Jerónimo carrying a red backpack. She had spent the day with her father visiting the workshop and listening to stories about Mateo. Rebeca showed her a photograph of the boy holding a wooden boat. Julia asked why he had never been mentioned at home until now.

“Because talking about him hurt,” Gabriel answered. “I thought staying silent would help me hold on to him. I was wrong.”

Julia set the photograph on the table.

“I'd like to get to know him through your memories, even the sad ones.”

That evening, they ate with Irene, Rebeca, and Eusebio. There was warm bread, thick soup, and friendly arguments about whether the town should spend money on fixing the fountain first or putting a roof over the school courtyard. Gabriel watched his daughter listen intently to stories told by neighbors she barely knew. For an instant, he was tempted to believe that everything was healing. Then he remembered Adela and the houses that had stood empty since the flood. Healing did not mean everyone would see the past in the same way.

When they were alone, Rebeca took a small reel of magnetic tape from a drawer. She had found it among Tomás's tools. Gabriel felt his stomach tighten.

“I don't know whether there's anything important on it,” she warned him. “Your father used to record instructions so he wouldn't forget the steps in his repairs. You can listen to it whenever you want. Or not at all.”

There was an old tape recorder in the workshop that only half worked. Gabriel cleaned the playback head and managed to get the tape moving. At first, he heard metal being struck, the screech of a saw, and Tomás's younger voice dictating measurements. Then, after a silence, a different recording began, made many years later.

“I've written reports asking for the high road to be repaired,” his father said in an aging voice. “I've spent my whole life going over the same things. I rang those bells because I thought I would wake everyone up. I didn't think enough about which way they would run. That responsibility is mine. I can't take responsibility for the current or for other people's decisions, but I can't hide what I did, either. Mateo died trying to help. It hurts to say that as if it were a sentence in a newspaper. He was my son. He liked sour oranges and whistled in his sleep. Gabriel had a right to be angry. I should have found a way to stay by his side even when he pushed me away.”

The tape stopped with a click. Gabriel sat motionless. He had found neither the confession he had imagined nor complete absolution. He had found a man who acknowledged his mistake but had not known how to bridge the distance between himself and his living son. Gabriel was angry about all the lost years; then he wept without trying to control his tears.

He went out into the courtyard. Irene was putting away the chairs after dinner. She saw his face and stopped working. Gabriel told her what he had just heard. She offered no comment on the recording. They sat beneath a cloud-covered sky, among the shadows of the trees.

“Tomorrow people will expect me to say something,” he murmured.

“You can tell them you're not ready.”

“I think I want to talk about Mateo. Without turning him into an explanation for anything.”

Irene nodded.

Before going to bed, Gabriel walked to the memorial plaque bearing the victims' names. Adela was there, laying a flower beside her sister's name. They greeted each other with a brief nod. Gabriel told her there would be one strike of the smaller bell the following day and that the courtyard would be open, but no one was obliged to attend.

“Thank you for letting me know,” Adela replied.

He hesitated.

“My father made a mistake. I don't expect that to change how you feel. I only wanted to tell you that I know that now.”

Adela looked at the plaque.

“I know things now that I didn't want to know before, either,” she said. “They don't always make life easier.”

They parted without an embrace or any promises. Gabriel walked home as a fine drizzle began to fall. In the workshop, he placed Tomás's wrench beside the photograph of Mateo. For the first time, he did not put either of them away in a closed box.

chapters.title: The Day the Bells Rang Again
chapters.content:
Sunday dawned bright after the rain. In the courtyard beside the bell tower, they set out simple benches, a sign displaying the safety procedures, and a table where the children exhibited their evacuation maps. The tower was still surrounded by a fence; the larger bell remained silent on its old support. Only the smaller one, mounted on a new, inspected frame, awaited its first strike. It did not look like a grand victory. It was a modest undertaking, paid for by contributions that still had to be accounted for, one by one.

Irene opened the gathering by explaining what had been accomplished and what still remained to be done. She thanked those who had donated money, those who had contributed their labor, and those who had pointed out risks. She reminded everyone that the ringing would not be an alarm and that emergency warnings would use other means. Several people nodded as they recognized the routes marked on the map.

Then Eusebio spoke. He had prepared no speech. He recounted how, on the day of the flood, he had tried to shout instructions from the hillside, and how for thirty years he had wondered whether he could have reached the others sooner. His voice trembled when he spoke the names of two neighbors who had died. He apologized for all the years he had confused avoiding the conversation with protecting the families.

Gabriel waited beside Julia, who held his hand. When his turn came, he looked at the familiar faces, the strangers, and the empty spaces where those who had chosen not to attend might have stood.

“My brother Mateo died here thirty years ago,” he began. “For a long time, I thought I could only remember him if I blamed my father. My father made the wrong decision when he used a signal not everyone understood. He also tried to help, and then lived with that mistake. I can't pretend he was innocent, and I can't reduce him to his worst moment. Either would be a way of no longer seeing him for who he was.”

He paused. Julia squeezed his fingers.

“Mateo didn't die to teach us a lesson. He was sixteen. He wanted to learn to drive, hated washing dishes, and once broke a school window with a ball. He deserved to go on living. So did the other eight people. If we do something good today, it won't be to justify what happened. It will be because we can still prevent someone from being left alone or confused when another storm comes.”

He lifted his eyes toward the stone arch.

“I can't explain why God allows certain losses. For years I believed that having faith meant finding an answer I could be satisfied with. I still don't have one. I'm only learning not to mistake God's silence for permission to abandon other people. And I'm learning to ask for help when the pain is greater than my strength.”

Not everyone reacted in the same way. Some wept; others remained silent. Adela was not among those present. Gabriel had set aside an unmarked chair, but he understood her absence and did not want to turn it into a symbol.

The bell was to be struck just once, slowly, using a manual mechanism that had been tested days earlier. Irene reminded everyone that there would be a few seconds' warning. A child raised a sign reading “ATTENTION,” followed by “CELEBRATORY BELL RINGING.” People had time to prepare themselves.

Eusebio handed the rope to Gabriel. Gabriel looked at Julia.

“Shall we hold it together?”

She nodded. They did not pull hard. The clapper moved and struck the bronze with a clear, brief note and a warm resonance. The sound crossed the courtyard, brushed the rooftops, and faded over the mountains. No one tried to ring it again. For a few moments, the only sounds were birds, footsteps, and the breathing of people who had waited far too long to hear a bell again.

Gabriel had feared the sound would bring back the night by the river. It did bring back some images: water striking wood, his mother's face, his childhood terror. But those images did not fill his whole mind. There was also his daughter's hand, the routes drawn by the schoolchildren, and the presence of neighbors who had worked together without agreeing on everything. The pain did not disappear. It found companionship.

When the gathering ended, Gabriel walked to the square. Adela stood outside the bakery, watching the children leave with their maps rolled up. She called him by name.

“I heard it from my house,” she said.

Gabriel did not know what to say.

“It hurt,” she added. “I suppose it will always hurt. But I'm grateful you gave us warning, that you didn't ring the larger bell, and that you taught the little ones what to do if the river rises.”

“It was the least we could do,” he replied.

Adela handed him a new photograph taken by her nephew at the ceremony. It showed Gabriel and Julia from behind, standing beside the frame, with the evacuation map visible beyond them.

“Everything doesn't have to be put right today,” she said.

He tucked the picture beside the old photograph of Mateo. They were two moments separated by thirty years. Neither canceled out the other.

As afternoon drew to a close, Gabriel called his daughter over to help him open the workshop windows. They had decided to keep the house for a few months and turn part of the space into a small place for learning: simple tools, bicycle repairs, and safety classes organized with the school. His job would remain in the city; he would visit on some weekends and share decisions with the people who lived there. He could not promise to be present all the time, but he wanted to stop making impossible promises and start keeping the concrete ones.

Julia found the wrench with the blue paint streak.

“Was this your dad's?”

“Yes. And sometimes my brother's. Dad used to lend it to us so we could learn.”

“Do you think he'd be happy?”

Gabriel thought of Tomás, of the tape, of his mistakes, and of everything neither of them had found time to say.

“I don't know,” he answered. “But I think he would have wanted us to learn to listen to each other before raising our voices.”

At dusk, from the workshop, the silhouette of the bell tower stood against a violet sky. The smaller bell had already sounded its one and only note of the day. The larger one would have to wait years, perhaps forever, until it could be safely restored. Gabriel did not feel that this waiting diminished the celebration.

Before closing up, he wrote on a chalkboard they intended to hang beside the door: “No one learns alone here.” Beneath it, he added the time of the first workshop and the date of the next evacuation drill. It was not a prayer written in solemn words, but as he turned out the lights, he offered one silently: that they might learn to care for one another, speak the truth in time, and never abandon those who were not yet ready to celebrate.

The bells of San Jerónimo had rung again—or at least one of them had—in a different way. They no longer asked the town to pretend its wounds had healed. They reminded its people that truly listening demanded something harder than recognizing a sound: staying, speaking clearly, and opening a path so others could reach safety.
